# W0013: field that no live code reads, or variant that no live code builds

A field of a class or a struct that live code builds is a warning when no live code reads it. The program still builds. A variant of an enum that live code builds is a warning when no live code builds that variant. Live code is as for [W0012](W0012.md). A write to a field, or a `+=` to it, does not read it.

These read each field of each struct that they show:

- a generated `print` or `eprint`
- an interpolation
- a generated `==`
- a call of the generated `to_string` or `eq`
- a conversion to an `any` type
- a type argument of a generic call

The struct can be in an array, an optional, an enum payload, another struct or a type argument. A class shows only its name, so a struct in a class is not read this way. A struct with a written `Display` shows its text. A struct with a written `Eq` compares as its `eq` says. In both cases the written method reads the fields that it names. A written `Display` does not stop a generated `==`, and a written `Eq` does not stop a generated `print`. The check cannot see what a generic function or an `any` value does with a struct, so it counts the struct as shown. The type arguments of a struct or an enum with a written conformance count as shown too, also under `dbg`. The written method can show them.

`dbg` shows the fields of a class or a struct. This holds when its operand is such a type, or holds one in an array, an optional, an enum payload or a struct. That is not a read: the warning for such a field shows the `dbg` call. The check reads types, not values, so the label says that `dbg` can show the field. An empty array or a `None` has no field to show. `dbg` shows a field that is a class by its name only. It shows a class or a struct with a written `to_string` by its text. So neither shows the fields. `print` and an interpolation show only the name of a class. A `dbg` in dead code does not count.

A pattern that names a variant does not build it. A use in dead code does not count, and the warning shows up to three such uses. A class, an enum or a struct that nothing builds gets W0012, not this warning. A field whose name starts with `_` gets no warning. The warning does not show while the program has an error. There is no fix, because only you know if the member is still necessary.

## Why

A field that nothing reads, or a variant that nothing builds, is a member that the type carries for nothing. Each value of the type holds the field's value, and each `match` on the enum needs an arm for the variant. But no part of the program uses them. They are often what a refactor leaves behind. A written `eq` reads the fields that it names, as any method does. Delete the member, or read it where the program needs it. To keep a field on purpose, start its name with `_`.

## Broken

```sisu
class Point {
    x: i64
    y: i64
}

fn main() {
    let p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
    print(p.x)
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
class Point {
    x: i64
    y: i64
}

fn main() {
    let p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
    print(p.x + p.y)
}
```
